name: Copperplate
tool: A flexible pointed nib, usually in an oblique holder.

name: Spencerian
tool: A fine, flexible pointed steel pen.

name: Modern
tool: A brush pen or a flexible pointed nib: press on the way down, lift to a hairline on the way up.

name: Italic
tool: A broad-edged pen held at about 35°.

name: Foundational
tool: A broad-edged pen held at a constant 30°. Some teachers flatten the pen for the thick diagonal of z and steepen it a little for v, w, x, y; here it stays at 30°, so z's diagonal comes out thin.

name: Roman Capitals
tool: A broad-edged pen (the models were laid out with a flat brush) held at about 27° throughout, the angle that tilts the O's stress back and makes the diagonals thick going down to the right and thin going down to the left. Scribes steepen the pen for the thin stems of N and M and flatten it for Z's diagonal; here the angle stays fixed, so those strokes come out heavier (N, M) or lighter (Z) than on the sheet.

name: Rustic Capitals
tool: A broad-edged pen held steeply, at 65° here: hairline stems, thick feet, arms and diagonals down to the right. The scribes turned the pen, about 70° for the uprights and 45° for horizontals and curves; with one angle per hand, 65° keeps the thin stems and thick feet that make the hand, so the curves of O, C, G and S are a little thinner than on the sheet.

name: Uncial
tool: A broad-edged pen held at a low angle, about 25° on this exemplar (the old books go as flat as 10-20°), so stems are heavy, level strokes about half as thick, and the thinnest point of a round letter is at its upper left.

name: Blackletter
tool: A broad-edged pen held at about 40°.

name: Bâtarde
tool: A broad-edged pen held at about 40°.

name: Fraktur
tool: A broad-edged pen held at about 45°.

name: Rotunda
tool: A broad-edged pen held fairly flat, at about 30° (the sheet: nearly parallel to the line, up to 30°).

name: Gothicized Italic
tool: A broad-edged pen held at about 35°.

name: Neuland
tool: A broad-edged pen used for weight, turned as the strokes need (or a heavy marker); modelled here as one even width with a square end, about a fifth of the capital height. The sheet's stems are nearly a third, but its turned pen makes the level strokes and the tops of the bowls much thinner; at that width one even stroke closes the counters, so the pen is lighter here to keep them open.
